advances: Closes every attained balanced active triple for which at most one of the three simultaneous selected outer lengths is positive. In the remaining one-positive-length payment pattern, the middle chord is genuinely displaced, with its displacement direction forced by an actual zero-payment endpoint row. A new weighted planar estimate bounds the relevant sector deficit by \(a_1/52\). Trimming the common endpoint bodies forces that same deficit above \(M/36\) under global failure, which is impossible in the accepted residual area range. The estimate is not an individual-sector inequality with zero error: an exact compatible, noncentral calibration below has a strictly positive sector deficit while satisfying all three full-section first-moment equations.
author: r132_weighted_sector
proof:
We first prove the planar assertion, including degenerate arrangements of the six radial endpoints. The proof will use only sector comparisons with a triangle. The subsequent endpoint-body containment will be established directly in \(A_1\).

Translate \(z\) to zero. Make an invertible linear change of coordinates sending the endpoint of the chord on \(g_2=0\) in \(\{g_1>0\}\) and the endpoint \(p_+\) to \((1,0)\) and \((0,1)\), respectively. The two bisected chords and (2) give the cyclic radial endpoints

\[
(1,0),\ (0,1),\ (-\xi,\eta),\ (-1,0),\ (0,-\nu),\ (\xi,-\eta),
\qquad \xi,\eta>0.
\tag{4}
\]

The halfplanes are \(Q_1=\{x\le0\}\), \(Q_2=\{y\le0\}\), and \(Q_3=\{\eta x+\xi y\ge0\}\). All areas change by the same positive factor under this coordinate change, and the division ratio \(\nu\) is unchanged.

First suppose the six points in (4) are in strictly convex position. The six consecutive turning determinants are positive. In particular,

\[
\begin{aligned}
&\xi+\eta-1>0,\qquad 1+\xi-\eta>0,\qquad 1+\eta-\xi>0,\\
&\nu+\eta-\nu\xi>0,\qquad
\nu+\nu\xi-\eta>0,\qquad
\nu\xi+\eta-\nu>0.
\end{aligned}
\tag{5}
\]

Retain the halfplane containing zero when each doubleton boundary arc is cut off along its radial endpoint chord. The intersection of the three retained halfplanes is

\[
P=\left\{(x,y):
\begin{aligned}
&\nu x+y\ge-\nu,\\
&\eta x+(\xi-1)y\le\eta,\\
&(\eta-1)x+\xi y\le\xi
\end{aligned}
\right\}.
\tag{6}
\]

The outward normals of the last two inequalities and then the first are \((\eta,\xi-1)\), \((\eta-1,\xi)\), and \((-\nu,-1)\). Their consecutive determinants are

\[
\xi+\eta-1,\qquad
1+\nu\xi-\eta,\qquad
\nu+\eta-\nu\xi.
\tag{7}
\]

All are positive. For the middle one, (5) and \(\nu\ge1\) give \(1+\nu\xi-\eta=(1+\xi-\eta)+(\nu-1)\xi>0\). The planar determinant identity therefore gives a strictly positive dependence among the three normals. A recession direction of (6) must pair nonpositively with each normal; the positive dependence forces all pairings to vanish. Two normals are independent, so that direction is zero. Thus \(P\) is bounded. It contains the convex hull of the six marks, with zero in its interior, and is consequently a nondegenerate triangle.

Its vertices occupy the singleton sectors with the indicated labels. Direct solution of the pairs of boundary equations gives

\[
\begin{aligned}
V_1={}&\left(-\frac{\xi(\nu+1)}{1+\nu\xi-\eta},
\frac{\nu(\xi+\eta-1)}{1+\nu\xi-\eta}\right),\\
V_2={}&\left(\frac{\nu\xi+\eta-\nu}{\nu+\eta-\nu\xi},
-\frac{2\eta\nu}{\nu+\eta-\nu\xi}\right),\\
V_3={}&\left(\frac{\xi(1+\eta-\xi)}{\xi+\eta-1},
\frac{\eta(1+\xi-\eta)}{\xi+\eta-1}\right).
\end{aligned}
\tag{8}
\]

The signs in (5), substituted into the three halfplane forms, verify these singleton labels. Each original radial endpoint remains the endpoint of the corresponding chord of \(P\): the central hexagon is contained in \(P\), and extension beyond a marked endpoint violates the retained inequality through that endpoint.

We justify the area comparisons explicitly. For adjacent radial endpoints \(p,q\) of any convex body containing zero, a body point beyond the line \(pq\), on the side not containing zero, must be in the open cone spanned by \(p,q\). In coordinates \(p=(1,0)\), \(q=(0,1)\), if \(X=(x,y)\) has \(x+y>1\) and \(x\le0\), the segment from \((1,0)\) to \(X\) meets the positive \(y\)-axis at height \(y/(1-x)>1\), contradicting the radial endpoint property. The case \(y\le0\) is symmetric. This proves the claim. It is the same elementary arc comparison used in accepted fact d6ab13d2d8067def, and it does not require chord bisection.

Applied to (6), the claim puts every singleton sector of \(K\) inside all three retained halfplanes. In a doubleton cone, its own retained inequality confines \(P\) to the triangle spanned by zero and that cone's two radial endpoints. That triangle is in the central hexagon and hence in \(P\), and it also lies in \(K\). Therefore, separately for every \(j\),

\[
s_j(K)\le s_j(P),\qquad
D_j(K)\ge D_j(P),\qquad
s_j(K)-D_j(K)\le s_j(P)-D_j(P).
\tag{9}
\]

We next establish the first two inequalities in (3) for this triangle. Normalize every area in the following calculation by \(|P|\). Let \(\theta_1,\theta_2,\theta_3\) be the barycentric coordinates of zero in \(P\). They are positive and sum to one. The bisected chord for \(Q_2\) has endpoints with the other barycentric coordinates \(2\theta_1\) and \(2\theta_3\), strictly below one; the analogous statement for \(Q_3\) also bounds \(2\theta_2\). Thus \(\theta_j<1/2\) for every \(j\). Put

\[
\varepsilon_j=1-2\theta_j>0,
\qquad \sum_j\varepsilon_j=1,
\qquad
\omega=\frac{\nu-1}{\nu+1}\in[0,2/7].
\tag{10}
\]

On the first chord, zero is the convex combination of its upper and lower endpoints with respective coefficients \(\nu/(1+\nu)\) and \(1/(1+\nu)\). The barycentric side fractions at the endpoints are therefore \(2\theta_3/(1+\omega)\) on \(V_1V_3\) and \(2\theta_2/(1-\omega)\) on \(V_1V_2\). The normalized cap areas are consequently

\[
\frac{|P\cap Q_1|}{|P|}
=\frac{4\theta_2\theta_3}{1-\omega^2},\qquad
\frac{|P\cap Q_2|}{|P|}=4\theta_1\theta_3,\qquad
\frac{|P\cap Q_3|}{|P|}=4\theta_1\theta_2.
\tag{11}
\]

To obtain a doubleton area, multiply the overlapping fraction of its side by the barycentric altitude from zero. This gives

\[
\begin{aligned}
\frac{D_1(P)}{|P|}&=\theta_1(1-2\theta_1),\\
\frac{D_2(P)}{|P|}&=\theta_2\left(2\theta_1+\frac{2\theta_3}{1+\omega}-1\right),\\
\frac{D_3(P)}{|P|}&=\theta_3\left(2\theta_1+\frac{2\theta_2}{1-\omega}-1\right).
\end{aligned}
\tag{12}
\]

Let \(k_P=\min_j(s_j(P)-D_j(P))/|P|\). The sector identity \(s_j-D_j=|P|-\sum_{i\ne j}|P\cap Q_i|\), together with (11), gives

\[
\begin{aligned}
\Delta&=\frac{(1-\varepsilon_2)(1-\varepsilon_3)\omega^2}{1-\omega^2},\\
k_P&=\min\{\varepsilon_1^2,\ \varepsilon_2^2-\Delta,\ \varepsilon_3^2-\Delta\},\\
\frac{D_1(P)+D_2(P)}{|P|}
&=\frac12\left(\varepsilon_1(1-\varepsilon_1)
+\varepsilon_2(1-\varepsilon_2)
-\frac{(1-\varepsilon_2)(1-\varepsilon_3)\omega}{1+\omega}\right),\\
\frac{D_3(P)}{|P|}
&=\frac12\varepsilon_3(1-\varepsilon_3)
+\frac{(1-\varepsilon_2)(1-\varepsilon_3)\omega}{2(1-\omega)}.
\end{aligned}
\tag{13}
\]

Since \(\omega\ge0\), the last expression is at least \(\varepsilon_3(\varepsilon_1+\varepsilon_2)/2\), which is at least \((\min_j\varepsilon_j)^2\). The definition of \(k_P\) then proves \(D_3(P)/|P|\ge k_P\).

For the pair estimate we prove the precise algebraic inequality \(11k_P\le6(D_1(P)+D_2(P))/|P|\). It is immediate if \(k_P\le0\), so suppose \(k_P>0\). Set \(u=\varepsilon_1\) and \(v=\min\{\varepsilon_2,\varepsilon_3\}\), so \(u>0\), \(v>0\), and \(u+2v\le1\). The product \((1-\varepsilon_2)(1-\varepsilon_3)\) equals \((u+v)(1-v)\). Moreover \(\varepsilon_2(1-\varepsilon_2)\ge v(1-v)\): if \(\varepsilon_2\) is the larger of the two coordinates, their difference after applying \(x\mapsto x(1-x)\) is \(u(\varepsilon_2-\varepsilon_3)\ge0\). Thus the pair area in (13) is at least

\[
\mathcal D(u,v)=\frac12\left(u(1-u)+v(1-v)
-\frac{(u+v)(1-v)\omega}{1+\omega}\right),
\tag{14}
\]

while \(k_P=\min\{u^2,v^2-(u+v)(1-v)\omega^2/(1-\omega^2)\}\).

The positivity of \(k_P\) implies \(v>\omega u\). This is automatic for \(\omega=0\). Otherwise, if \(v\le\omega u\), the inequality \(u+2v\le1\) gives \(v\le\omega/(1+2\omega)<\omega\), and

\[
v^2-\frac{(u+v)(1-v)\omega^2}{1-\omega^2}
\le v^2-\frac{v(1-v)\omega}{1-\omega}
=\frac{v(v-\omega)}{1-\omega}<0,
\]

contrary to \(k_P>0\). We may therefore work on the closed polygon defined by \(u,v\ge0\), \(u+2v\le1\), and \(v\ge\omega u\).

For fixed \(\omega\), the two possible differences \(6\mathcal D-11k_P\) are

\[
\begin{aligned}
F_1(u,v)&=3u-14u^2+3v-3v^2
-3\gamma_\omega(u+v)(1-v),\\
F_2(u,v)&=3u-3u^2+3v-14v^2
+R_\omega(u+v)(1-v),\\
\gamma_\omega&=\frac{\omega}{1+\omega},
\qquad R_\omega=\frac{\omega(14\omega-3)}{1-\omega^2}.
\end{aligned}
\tag{15}
\]

Here \(F_1\) applies when \(u^2\) is the minimum, and \(F_2\) when the other expression is the minimum. Both polynomials are concave in \((u,v)\). Indeed, \(0\le\gamma_\omega\le2/9\) and \(-1<R_\omega<1\) for \(0\le\omega\le2/7\). For the latter bound, the numerator is between \(-6/7\) and \(2/7\), while the denominator is at least \(45/49\), giving the stronger bounds \(-14/15\le R_\omega\le14/45\). Their Hessians are

\[
\begin{pmatrix}-28&3\gamma_\omega\\3\gamma_\omega&-6+6\gamma_\omega\end{pmatrix},
\qquad
\begin{pmatrix}-6&-R_\omega\\-R_\omega&-28-2R_\omega\end{pmatrix}.
\tag{16}
\]

Both have negative first diagonal entry and positive determinant. For the first, the determinant is at least \(1172/9>0\); for the second it is at least \(155>0\).

The switch between the two minima is a straight line, because

\[
u^2-v^2+\frac{(u+v)(1-v)\omega^2}{1-\omega^2}
=\frac{u+v}{1-\omega^2}
\bigl((1-\omega^2)u-v+\omega^2\bigr).
\tag{17}
\]

Put \(u_*=(1-2\omega^2)/(3-2\omega^2)\) and \(v_*=1/(3-2\omega^2)\). The region for \(F_1\) is the triangle with vertices \((0,\omega^2)\), \((0,1/2)\), and \((u_*,v_*)\). The condition \(v\ge\omega u\) is automatic there, since \(1-\omega^2>\omega\). The region for \(F_2\) is the quadrilateral with vertices

\[
(0,0),\quad (0,\omega^2),\quad (u_*,v_*),\quad
\left(\frac1{1+2\omega},\frac{\omega}{1+2\omega}\right).
\tag{18}
\]

At \(\omega=0\), repeated vertices are simply omitted. These vertex lists follow by intersecting the switch line with \(u=0\) and \(u+2v=1\), and intersecting \(v=\omega u\) with \(u+2v=1\).

A concave function on a polygon is bounded below by the minimum of its vertex values. At \((0,0)\) the relevant value is zero. At \((0,\omega^2)\) the two minima agree and vanish, so the common value is \(6\mathcal D=3\omega^2(1-\omega^2)/(1+\omega)\ge0\). At \((0,1/2)\), \(F_1=3/(4(1+\omega))>0\). At the last vertex in (18), the second doubleton term in (14) is zero, whereas its candidate minimum is \(v(v-\omega)/(1-\omega)\le0\). Thus \(F_2\ge0\) there as well. Finally, direct substitution at \((u_*,v_*)\) gives the common value

\[
\begin{aligned}
F_1(u_*,v_*)=F_2(u_*,v_*)
&=\frac{1-12\omega+38\omega^2+12\omega^3-56\omega^4}{(3-2\omega^2)^2},\\
1-12\omega+38\omega^2+12\omega^3-56\omega^4
&=(1-6\omega)^2+2\omega^2(1+6\omega-28\omega^2)>0.
\end{aligned}
\tag{19}
\]

For the last strict inequality, the concave quadratic \(1+6\omega-28\omega^2\) is at least \(3/7\) on \([0,2/7]\); at \(\omega=0\) the first square equals one. Hence both regions have nonnegative relevant polynomial. This proves \(11k_P\le6\mathcal D\), and therefore proves the pair estimate in the triangle.

Restore the area factor. By (9), \(k\le |P|k_P\), while each doubleton area of \(K\) is at least its counterpart in \(P\). Thus the two triangle inequalities give \(D_3(K)\ge k\) and \(D_1(K)+D_2(K)\ge11k/6\). If \(k\le0\), the last assertion of (3) is immediate. If \(k>0\), the sector partition and these two bounds give

\[
\begin{aligned}
|K|-52(2k-D_1-D_2)
&=\sum_j(s_j-D_j)+2D_3+54(D_1+D_2)-104k\\
&\ge54(D_1+D_2)-99k\ge0.
\end{aligned}
\tag{20}
\]

This proves (3) when the marks are in strictly convex position.

Here is a limit argument that preserves the chord conditions in every remaining case. Let \(p_K\) be the gauge of \(K\) about zero, so \(p_K(x)=\inf\{r>0:x\in rK\}\), and for \(\epsilon>0\) put \(K_\epsilon=\{x:p_K(x)+\epsilon\|x\|\le1\}\). Convexity and positive homogeneity of the gauge follow directly from convexity of \(K\). The Euclidean norm is strictly convex on pairs of points that are not positively collinear. Two distinct boundary points of this homogeneous sublevel set cannot be positively collinear, so \(K_\epsilon\) is strictly convex. In particular its six radial marks are in strictly convex position, and the preceding argument applies to it even though it need not be polygonal; that argument used only convexity.

A radial length \(r\) of \(K\) becomes \(r/(1+\epsilon r)\). Each bisected chord stays bisected. If the positive length on the first chord is \(r_+\), its new division ratio is \(\nu(1+\epsilon r_+)/(1+\epsilon\nu r_+)\), lying in \([1,\nu]\). Thus (2) also persists. As \(\epsilon\downarrow0\), these bodies increase to the interior of \(K\), possibly together with boundary points. A convex body's boundary has planar area zero, so each of the six sector areas converges to its area in \(K\). Passing to the limit in (3) proves the planar assertion with collinear radial marks as well.

We now prove the three-slice conclusion. Suppose, to the contrary, that every point of \(S\) has depth below \(t\). Accepted facts 15bb2c1680a0254e and 291c24bb45bd4946 give

\[
0<m<\frac{3M}{8},\qquad M-m<a_1<M+m,
\qquad d<t<M.
\tag{21}
\]

The last inequality follows from \(t<4(M+m)/9\le8M/9\). Reflect the height coordinate if necessary so that \(a_0=M\) and \(a_2=m\); this exchanges endpoint bodies, negates every slope, and preserves all middle and selected-section conclusions. Retain the same notation for the reflected objects.

Use \(g_j(w)=\alpha_jq_j\cdot(w-z)\), \(\sigma_j=\alpha_j\lambda_j\), and \(Q_j=\{g_j\le0\}\). Let \(e_j\) be the actual total area contributed by the endpoints in row \(j\). The middle cap area is \(d-e_j\). Each payment satisfies \(0\le e_j\le m\): keeping its normal and \(z\) fixed, a sufficiently negative finite height slope makes the large-endpoint contribution zero and the small-endpoint contribution exactly \(m\), leaving the middle cap unchanged. The new halfspace contains \((1,z)\), so its mass \(d-e_j+m\) cannot be less than \(d\).

If all selected lengths vanish, accepted fact d6ab13d2d8067def already gives a point of depth at least \(t\), a contradiction. There is therefore exactly one positive selected length; relabel it as \(\ell_1>0\), with \(\ell_2=\ell_3=0\). By the precise selection convention in e4a8e2c026dd7346, neither endpoint boundary in rows 2 and 3 is transverse. Its cap area is therefore zero or the full slice area. A full contribution \(M\) is impossible by (21), so \(e_2,e_3\in\{0,m\}\). Also \(c_{12}=c_{13}=z\), so the corresponding full middle chords are bisected.

The pattern \(e_2=e_3=0\) is impossible. In a zero-payment row both endpoint bodies lie in the closed complements of their endpoint halfplanes: any point strictly on the selected side would give positive area by convexity and two-dimensionality. Hence \(B=(A_0+A_2)/2\) lies in \(\{g_2\ge0,g_3\ge0\}\). Its intersection with \(g_1=0\) is contained in \(g_2=g_3=0\), namely \(\{z\}\). But the selected midpoint segment \((E_{01}+E_{21})/2\) has positive length \(\ell_1\) and lies in \(B\cap\{g_1=0\}\), a contradiction.

The pattern \(e_2=e_3=m\) is impossible as well. The planar cap inequality of accepted fact 851e063a1b9908a3, with cap areas \(d-e_1,d-m,d-m\), gives \(9d\ge4a_1+5e_1+4m\ge4(a_1+m)>2T\), contradicting \(d<t\). Here that accepted fact's cap-area notation is mapped to \(d-e_j\), not to the canonical chord lengths \(b_j\).

Consequently, after possibly exchanging rows 2 and 3, the payment vector is \((e,0,m)\), with \(0\le e\le m\). If \(e=m\), the same accepted planar cap inequality again gives \(9d\ge4(a_1+m)>2T\). Thus

\[
(e_1,e_2,e_3)=(e,0,m),\qquad 0\le e<m,
\qquad n:=m-e>0.
\tag{22}
\]

The zero payment in row 2 forces \(B\subseteq\{g_2\ge0\}\). Use the coordinates of the planar assertion, with \(z=0\), \(g_1=0\) the vertical line and \(g_2=0\) the horizontal line. The positive-length midpoint segment \((E_{01}+E_{21})/2\) lies on the nonnegative vertical ray. Its midpoint has strictly positive vertical coordinate. The actual moment equation (1) forces the full first middle chord midpoint to have strictly negative vertical coordinate. Thus its negative radial length is larger than its positive radial length. If their ratio is \(\nu\), then the displacement bound in (1) gives

\[
0<\frac{\nu-1}{\nu+1}
=\frac{2\|c_{11}-z\|}{b_1}
\le2-\sqrt3<\frac27.
\tag{23}
\]

The last strict comparison follows from \(\sqrt3>12/7\). In particular \(1<\nu<9/5\). Both the direction and the size of this displacement have therefore been obtained from the actual common midpoint segment and its first moment. The planar assertion applies with precisely these row labels.

Let \(s_j,D_j\) now denote the sectors of \(A_1\). The exact partition by the concurrent fan gives

\[
\begin{aligned}
s_1-D_1&=a_1-2d+m,\\
s_2-D_2&=a_1-2d+e+m,\\
s_3-D_3&=a_1-2d+e.
\end{aligned}
\tag{24}
\]

Thus \(k=\min_j(s_j-D_j)=a_1-2d+e\). Put \(L=2k-D_1-D_2\). By (3), \(L\le a_1/52\). The row-3 cap identity also gives the exact relation

\[
s_3=d-m-D_1-D_2=5d-2a_1-2e-m+L.
\tag{25}
\]

We next use both common endpoint bodies to pay for this allowance. Trim each endpoint by the closed complements of rows 1 and 2. If \(x\) is the sum of the two corresponding large-endpoint cap areas and \(y\) the sum of the two small-endpoint cap areas, then \(x,y\ge0\) and \(x+y=e\), because row 2 has payment zero. The trimmed convex polygons \(K_0,K_2\) satisfy \(|K_0|\ge M-x>0\) and \(|K_2|\ge m-y>0\). Their midpoint body \(\widetilde B=(K_0+K_2)/2\) is contained in \(A_1\), and averaging the two complementary inequalities in each of rows 1 and 2 places it in \(\{g_1\ge0,g_2\ge0\}\), the closure of singleton sector 3.

Apply the necessity direction of accepted fact d7bdfc054d5093e8 to \(K_0,\widetilde B,K_2\). They are the three integer-height sections of the convex hull of the two endpoint polygons, and all are two-dimensional. It yields

\[
s_3\ge |\widetilde B|
\ge\frac{(\sqrt{M-x}+\sqrt{m-y})^2}{4}
\ge\frac{(\sqrt M+\sqrt n)^2}{4}.
\tag{26}
\]

For the last inequality, \(m-y=n+x\), and \((M-x)(n+x)-Mn=x(M-n-x)\ge0\), since \(0\le x\le e=m-n\le M-n\). The two radicands have sum \(M+n\), which proves the comparison after expanding both squares. This is a bound on the actual trimmed endpoint bodies, with no replacement of their shapes by independent segment budgets.

On the other hand, (21), (22), and (25) give

\[
\begin{aligned}
s_3
&<\frac{10M+10m-8a_1}{9}-2e-m+L\\
&<\frac{2M}{9}+m-2e+L
\le\frac{2M}{9}+n+L.
\end{aligned}
\tag{27}
\]

Combining (26) and (27) and multiplying by 36 gives

\[
36L>M+18\sqrt{Mn}-27n>M.
\tag{28}
\]

The second strict inequality uses \(0<n\le m<3M/8<4M/9\), which implies \(27n<18\sqrt{Mn}\). But the planar upper bound and (21) give

\[
L\le\frac{a_1}{52}
<\frac{11M}{416}<\frac{M}{36},
\tag{29}
\]

where \(11\cdot36=396<416\). Equations (28) and (29) contradict one another. This proves the stated one-positive-length exclusion.

For an exact noncentral calibration of the weighted step, take the middle triangle

\[
A_1=P=\{(x,y):7x+5y\ge-7,\ 39x-11y\le39,\ -x+29y\le29\},
\tag{30}
\]

with fan \(Q_1=\{x\le0\}\), \(Q_2=\{y\le0\}\), \(Q_3=\{39x+29y\ge0\}\), centered at zero. Its vertices are \((-87/52,49/52)\), \((59/136,-273/136)\), and \((145/112,117/112)\). The six marks have \(\xi=29/40\), \(\eta=39/40\), and \(\nu=7/5\). Exact triangle areas give

\[
\begin{aligned}
|P|&=\frac{111005}{24752},\\
(D_1,D_2,D_3)&=\left(\frac{39}{80},\frac{29}{80},\frac7{10}\right),\\
(s_1-D_1,s_2-D_2,s_3-D_3)
&=\left(\frac{119}{260},\frac{311}{680},\frac{263}{560}\right),\\
2\min_j(s_j-D_j)-D_1-D_2&=\frac{11}{170}>0.
\end{aligned}
\tag{31}
\]

These marks and their first moments are compatible with actual common endpoint bodies. Take

\[
\begin{aligned}
A_0&=[-1001/1000,-4/5]\times[1/5,3/5],\\
A_2&=[999/1000,51/50]\times[3/5,1].
\end{aligned}
\tag{32}
\]

Their midpoint sum is the rectangle \([-1/1000,11/100]\times[2/5,4/5]\), which satisfies all three inequalities in (30). Use the three spatial cuts \(x-(h-1)\le0\), \(y\le0\), and \(39x+29y\ge0\). Their positively balanced concurrent planar forms can be taken proportional to \(39x\), \(29y\), and \(-39x-29y\), with the corresponding unit-normal weights.

The first full outer chords have length \(2/5\), with midpoints \((-1,2/5)\) and \((1,4/5)\). The first full middle chord has length \(12/5\) and midpoint \((0,-1/5)\), so its total vector first moment vanishes exactly: its vertical component is \((12/5)(-1/5)+2(2/5)(3/5)=0\), and the horizontal components cancel. The other two outer sections are empty; their middle chords are bisected and their full first moments are zero. Thus the selected lengths are \((2/5,0,0)\) with the required full-section convention. The payments are \((1/1250,0,21/2500)\), and the endpoint areas are \(201/2500\) and \(21/2500\).

This calibration verifies that the zero-loss pair bound fails even with actual compatible endpoint segments and all three first-moment balances. It is not an attained equal-mass active family and does not satisfy the residual area strip. The proved weighted inequality does hold: \(|P|-52(11/170)=138609/123760>0\). All rational areas, section identities, and the polynomial identity (19) can be checked by direct arithmetic; they were also independently audited with exact rational polyhedra and symbolic arithmetic in SageMath 10.8. No computational search or numerical infeasibility result is used in the proof.
statement:
Let \(C\) satisfy the locked three-slice problem, with slices \(A_0,A_1,A_2\), areas \(a_i=|A_i|\), total area \(T=a_0+a_1+a_2\), endpoint areas \(M=\max\{a_0,a_2\}\), \(m=\min\{a_0,a_2\}\), and \(t=2T/9\). Suppose there are attained active-cut and simultaneous selected-section objects as in accepted fact e4a8e2c026dd7346. Thus \(z\in\operatorname{int}A_1\), \(d=h_S((1,z))=\max_{w\in A_1}h_S((1,w))\), the pairwise nonparallel unit normals \(q_j\) have positive weights \(\alpha_j\) satisfying \(\sum_j\alpha_j=1\) and \(\sum_j\alpha_jq_j=0\), and the cuts

\[
\widehat H_j=\{(h,w):q_j\cdot(w-z)+\lambda_j(h-1)\le0\}
\qquad(j=1,2,3)
\]

all have mass \(d\). Write \(L_{ij}\) for their full slice boundary sections, \(b_j=\mathcal H_1(L_{1j})>0\) for the middle chord lengths, and \(c_{1j}\) for the middle chord midpoints. The simultaneous selected segments \(E_{0j}\subseteq L_{0j}\) and \(E_{2j}\subseteq L_{2j}\) have equal lengths \(\ell_j\), satisfy the full vector first-moment balance of that accepted fact, and use its exact selection convention: a transverse outer section is selected in full; a supporting edge may supply a subsegment; an empty or point section supplies zero selected length. In particular, when \(\ell_j>0\), their midpoint sum has length \(\ell_j\), lies in \(L_{1j}\), and its midpoint \(c_j\) satisfies

\[
b_j(c_{1j}-z)+2\ell_j(c_j-z)=0,
\qquad
\|c_{1j}-z\|\le\left(1-\frac{\sqrt3}{2}\right)b_j.
\tag{1}
\]

If at most one of \(\ell_1,\ell_2,\ell_3\) is positive, then some \(y\in S\) has \(h_S(y)\ge t\).

A weighted planar assertion used in the proof is the following. Let \(K\) be a compact two-dimensional convex body, let \(z\in\operatorname{int}K\), and let \(g_1,g_2,g_3\) be pairwise nonparallel affine forms vanishing at \(z\), with \(g_1+g_2+g_3=0\). Put \(Q_j=\{g_j\le0\}\). Let \(s_j\) be the area in \(K\) belonging only to \(Q_j\), and let \(D_j\) be the area belonging to the other two halfplanes. Suppose the full chords on \(g_2=0\) and \(g_3=0\) are bisected by \(z\). On the remaining chord, let \(p_+\) be its endpoint in \(\{g_2>0\}\), and let \(p_-\) be its endpoint in \(\{g_2<0\}\). Suppose

\[
1\le\nu:=\frac{\|p_--z\|}{\|p_+-z\|}\le\frac95.
\tag{2}
\]

For \(k=\min_j(s_j-D_j)\), one has

\[
D_3\ge k,
\qquad D_1+D_2\ge\frac{11}{6}k,
\qquad
2k-D_1-D_2\le\frac{|K|}{52}.
\tag{3}
\]

Here \(D_j\) are sector areas, not the attained mixed-integer depth \(d\); the affine forms in the application are the concurrent \(g_j=\alpha_jq_j\cdot(w-z)\), whose sum is zero.
